title: Outlook for the U.S. and Alaskan Economies
summary: Cook takes the decisive step her July 15 speech stopped short of: she names the instrument. Where July closed on a vague 'If we do not see signs of disinflation soon, I am prepared to act,' Anchorage says it explicitly — 'I am prepared to act by raising rates, if necessary' and 'I would support an increase, if it becomes necessary to bring inflation down.' That makes her, alongside the three July dissenters, the first Governor outside the dissent bloc to put a hike on the table in her own words, and it comes wrapped in an urgency argument: with five years of above-target inflation, 'the risk grows that higher inflation may become entrenched in price- and wage-setting behavior,' so 'while we might be able to afford to wait for longer in a different environment, we do not have that luxury in this one.' The inflation diagnosis is unchanged from July — PCE 3.7% ('nearly double our target'), core 3.3%, and energy 'is not the only factor' — with the AI capex buildout still treated as a genuine price shock (semis, high-tech equipment, software, utilities) rather than only a productivity story, alongside the Middle East conflict as the year's two unexpected sources of price pressure. Labor stays where she left it: 4.2% unemployment at roughly the natural rate, low claims, >100k/month payrolls in Q2, low-hire/low-fire read as structural, and AI job risk 'significant' but 'not grown over the past year' — so 'the balance of risks' has 'shifted toward inflation and away from the labor market.' What is genuinely NEW on the dovish side is a three-part self-correction list that did not exist in July: tariff price-level effects are 'mostly behind us' and 'may no longer provide much inflationary push going forward'; oil is expected by many forecasters to 'come down by the end of the year, providing some deflationary relief'; and AI-driven goods pressure 'will ease' as supply chains adjust. She is explicit that the hike 'may not' be necessary because of them, and those three reasons are why she backed the July hold. Net: a hawkish escalation in the ACTION space (hike named, entrenchment clock running) partly offset by a newly articulated benign inflation path — the two big drivers she used to score hawkish, tariffs and oil, have flipped to disinflationary in her own telling, leaving underlying broadening and the AI capex shock carrying the hawkish case. Roughly a third of the speech is Alaska-specific and a consumer-sentiment digression whose policy conclusion is the same commitment device: 'the best thing we can do in our roles is to ensure that inflation returns to and stays at target.'

key_quotes.quote: As such, I am prepared to act by raising rates, if necessary. The labor market and output growth are currently stable. I would consider how a rate increase could negatively affect that stability. Still, I would support an increase, if it becomes necessary to bring inflation down.
key_quotes.context: THE mover vs July 15, which used only the ambiguous 'prepared to act'; she now names hikes as the instrument and says she would support one, while acknowledging the cost to a stable labor market and output

key_quotes.quote: With five years of above-target inflation, the risk grows that higher inflation may become entrenched in price- and wage-setting behavior, leading to persistence that would be much harder for us to attack. The longer inflation is above target, the more likely this scenario becomes. Thus, while we might be able to afford to wait for longer in a different environment, we do not have that luxury in this one.
key_quotes.context: The urgency clause — an explicit entrenchment/expectations argument that puts a clock on the patient hold

key_quotes.quote: It may not. Some disinflationary forces are already in play, which could push inflation toward our target without a rate increase.
key_quotes.context: The new dovish counterweight, absent in July: she lays out three self-correcting forces (tariff base effects dropping out, oil expected lower by year-end, AI goods pressure easing as supply chains adjust) and says they are why 'I felt it was appropriate not to change rates'

key_quotes.quote: First, the effects of tariffs announced last year on the price level are mostly behind us. So even though those tariffs account for a lot of the elevated inflation seen in 12-month changes, they may no longer provide much inflationary push going forward.
key_quotes.context: Driver flip: tariffs scored hawkish for her through July, now framed as a source of mechanical disinflation as base effects roll out of the window

key_quotes.quote: Taken together, these developments have shifted the balance of risks toward inflation and away from the labor market.
key_quotes.context: Same risk-balance verdict as July 15, now attributed to the two unexpected price shocks of 2026 — the Middle East conflict and the AI capex buildout, which 'lifted prices for semiconductors, high-tech equipment, software, and utilities'

key_quotes.quote: I still see this development as a significant risk but one that has not grown over the past year.
key_quotes.context: On AI job displacement — keeps the labor-side counterweight collapsed: unemployment 4.2% at roughly the natural rate, low claims, >100k/month payrolls in Q2, low-hire/low-fire read as structural rather than a downturn signal
